newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb hardliners consult Milosevic over feud.
newsitem.headline: Serb hardliners consult Milosevic over feud.

text.p: Bosnian Serb hardliners loyal to indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic sought help from Serbia in their power struggle with President Biljana Plavsic.

Trying to gain the upper hand in the confrontation, Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of Bosnia's collective presidency, travelled to Belgrade on Wednesday to consult with Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
Both men called for "unity" among Bosnian Serb leaders after the meeting which Plavsic dismissed as an attempt by the Serbian leader to interfere in Bosnia's Serb republic.
Plavsic rejected Milosevic's invitation to mediate in the conflict and instead held a rally attended by thousands of supporters in the eastern town of Bijeljina.
The Bosnian Serb leader is waging a battle with her former associates grouped around ex-president Karadzic, accusing them of large-scale corruption.
By meeting Milosevic, the hardliners were trying to portray Plavsic as an isolated figure who was unwilling to compromise.
Milosevic armed separatist Serb forces in their war against Bosnian independence and the impoverished Bosnian Serb republic still depends on economic ties to Serbian-led Yugoslavia for its survival.
Diplomats say Milosevic has restored links with Karadzic's allies since he forced them to sign the 1995 Dayton peace accords against their will.

Plavsic dissolved the Bosnian Serb assembly last week and called for general elections. Karadzic loyalists ignored her decision and held an assembly session anyway, rewriting laws to enable her recall and strip her of powers.
Although Plavsic has damaged the hardliners by blowing the whistle on war profiteering, Karadzic's allies still control a large police force and the official television network.
Karadzic loyalists appeared confident they would win a favourable decision from the Serb constitutional court, which was expected to rule soon on Plavsic's moves.
Western governments say Plavsic acted legally when she dissolved the parliament but they were concerned that two competing authorities would emerge if the conflict continued.
U.S. President Bill Clinton lent his voice to Western support for Plavsic at a NATO summit in Madrid.
"We support Mrs Plavsic in what she is trying to do, we oppose the unconstitutional efforts to usurp her authority," Clinton told reporters.
Clinton sidestepped questions about whether NATO peacekeeping troops would be ordered to arrest Karadzic and other suspects charged by the U.N. war crimes tribunal.
He said it would be "inappropriate" to comment on whether "snatch squads" should be sent to seize them.
Milosevic and Plavsic, longtime political foes, jousted through public statements.
Plavsic denied she was trying to pit the western part of the Serb republic around the town of Banja Luka against the eastern region ruled from Pale, outside Sarajevo.

She said that the conflict was about "whether a state governed by law will finally be created here or whether the Serb republic will continue to be the exclusive property of a single party steeped in crime".

Plavsic remains a nationalist ideologue who supported wartime "ethnic cleansing" of Moslems and Croats, but she has advocated cooperation with international peacemaking to win badly needed reconstruction funds for Serb territory.
Western envoys blasted Karadzic's party for denying Plavsic access to television and said their media coverage was a "disgrace to journalism".

A spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, warned Serb authorities that Westendorp retained the right to curtail or suspend any media outlet which violated the peace agreement.
Westendorp's office declined to elaborate on what options were being considered.
